title: Doing Social Media in the AI Era: Your Boss Is More Hopeless Than the Algorithm
dek: The real AI shock to marketing teams comes from the boss: outsource your intuition to Claude, approve only what Copilot generates, and staff end up disguising their own ideas as Copilot screenshots to get sign-off.
why: Medium information density, but Rachel's first-hand interviews about "bosses with AI brain" and the Threads algorithm mechanics are industry details you won't hear anywhere else.
who: Brand social and content marketing practitioners, MCN and creator-economy investors, and anyone who wants to know how AI is changing the creative industries from inside the organisation.
skip: The first two minutes of guest introductions and the Coca-Cola truck bit — jump straight to 04:06.

points.h: Bosses have outsourced their intuition to Claude
points.body: Rachel interviewed roughly a hundred marketers and found that the main path AI takes into a team isn't tool procurement — it's the boss. A social media manager carefully makes a funny meme, sends it to the boss, and the boss drops it into Claude to ask "is this funny?" Even more absurd: some marketers discovered their boss only approves ideas that come from Copilot, so they first mock their own ideas up to look like a Copilot interface, then send that for approval. Rachel says what's underneath is the boss outsourcing their entire intuitive judgment to AI, with no training or guardrails in the team on how to use AI at all — she contrasts it with her own experience spending months learning Asana at Condé Nast.

points.h: Consumers don't hate AI, they hate being fooled
points.body: Taylor points out an overlooked fact: plenty of YouTubers now read AI-generated scripts straight to camera, and the comments still praise the "brilliant analysis, well-written script." In other words, when people don't know they're consuming AI content, they actually like it. What triggers rage isn't AI itself but the feeling of having been played. Rachel adds the explanation for this double standard: an AI fruit romance meme like Fruit Love Island is low-stakes meme content, and nobody cares about the craft of a meme; but when a brand you pay money to uses AI to generate a menu, you start wondering how much else it's cutting corners on in the product. The same person can denounce a brand for using AI while forwarding an AI fruit meme to a friend.

points.h: How-to creators are the first to be replaced by AI
points.body: Rachel splits creators into two groups. Those who built their following on how-to content are most at risk — from the earliest YouTube beauty tutorials onward, the democratisation of media ran along this path, but for questions like "how do I fix the dishwasher," AI is the better authority and people will just ask it. Taylor gives the example of her own mother, who recently fixed a toilet with ChatGPT and was very proud of it — unthinkable before. The other group is actually safer: people doing deep parasocial content, commentary, things that aren't easily replicated can use these tools to make better content. The test is whether the content itself can be copied.

points.h: Anti-data-center and anti-extinction crowds never allied
points.body: Taylor observes that people opposed to data centers and people worried about AI wiping out humanity are two groups with completely different motivations, and they still haven't formed any coherent alliance — she half-jokingly says they should team up, but their interests diverge too much. Her own position is clear: AI won't kill us, "it's actually really hard to kill all humans on Earth, even if we wanted to." What she thinks genuinely deserves scrutiny is how people anthropomorphise AI and grant these products agency — especially dangerous in policy debates about assigning responsibility, because they are computer programs, not living things. She also quotes a former FTC commissioner: we survived the Black Death, and that only killed 50% of people.

points.h: AI accounts are pulling Instagram's slot machine
points.body: Taylor thinks Meta is in a hard spot because it is essentially a 2010s social network whose influence peaked in the 2010s, while Google is better positioned than Meta. In the short term, AI's impact on platforms is about scale and speed: one AI account can post 50 times a day, which is like constantly pulling Instagram's slot machine — eventually something hits. She looked at the 20 most-viewed reels at the time, and two or three were AI-generated, all of them very new. One used a "behind the scenes" framing to show how a crew films ocean waves and how the waves wash away a house — essentially using "proof of authenticity" as a shell to manufacture confusion. Her read: this is monetising confusion, with short-term gains and a very bad long-term outcome.

points.h: Threads is the most toxic social platform
points.body: Taylor says she recently posted hot takes calling Threads the most toxic social platform to date, far more toxic than Twitter — "Twitter compared to Threads is a beautiful wonderland." The mechanism is that the algorithm prioritises replies extremely heavily, so you get dropped straight into someone's angry reply about something, which in turn feeds the algorithm and quickly escalates into groupthink pile-ons. She also points out that Threads' AI-generated news summaries "are just lying, straight-up making things up." Asked who uses Threads, her answer is: her mom.

points.h: The growth secret is turning your account into a series
points.body: Asked how to grow an audience in the AI era, Rachel says the accounts growing now all have a clear through-line of familiarity in their content, like they're making their own TV show. Her example is a restaurant chef filming himself cooking while wearing Meta glasses, who grew to about 500,000 followers in two or three months under the account name Gil Holy Cooks, posting one episode a day. Taylor adds that content is becoming serialised across the board, and you really have to think about how to entertain people; the era of "share your life" is clearly declining, and in 2026 you should not become a lifestyle influencer — there's a lot of anger directed at those people.

points.h: Instagram handed out an official format division-of-labour chart
points.body: Rachel says Instagram once shared a very useful chart with her readers explaining what each content format is for: carousels and reels are for reaching new audiences and get pushed to non-followers, and what the current algorithm really feeds on is non-follower views — if your content only makes sense to your own audience, the platform judges it "not entertaining enough" and withholds main-feed distribution. Single-image posts serve only your existing audience. Stories and DMs are treated by the platform as where community happens. She also quotes Adam Mosseri on Bloomberg Screen Time: the "social" in social media is no longer about sharing family photos but about DMing friends the things that remind you of them. She finds that a shame, but it does clarify what "social" now means on social media.

Instagram's short-video format, pushed mainly to non-followers just like carousels.
Mass-generated, low-quality, volume-over-substance AI content, such as Fruit Love Island.
